sovereign_country.strategic_role: 北美成熟市场、联邦与省两级公司实体设立（EPC合规）

business_scope.primary_industry_name: Online Retail of Cosmetics and Personal Care Products

applicable_bilateral_investment_treaties: Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP)
Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) between Canada and the EU
Canada-China Foreign Investment Promotion and Protection Agreement (FIPA)

ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA), S.C. 2000, c. 17, as amended, and its associated regulations; Business Corporations Act (Alberta), R.S.A. 2000, c. B-9, Part 17.1 (Register of Individuals with Significant Control); Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44, s. 21.1 (for federal corporations); Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part II.1; Special Economic Measures Act, S.C. 1992, c. 17; Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act, S.C. 2011, c. 31, s. 2.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certified true copy of passport or national identity document of each director, shareholder and individual with significant control
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Passport issuing authority or Notary Public in the country of origin
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille for Hague Convention countries; otherwise Consular Legalization through the Canadian Embassy or High Commission

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Good Standing / Certificate of Corporate Existence for any corporate shareholder
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Corporate registry of the foreign shareholder's home jurisdiction
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille or Consular Legalization, as applicable

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Incumbency / Register of Directors and Officers for any parent entity
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Corporate registry or registered agent of the parent entity

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Notarized Power of Attorney appointing the Alberta resident incorporator or registered agent
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary Public in the country of origin
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille; Consular Legalization if required by the agent or registry

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certified UBO Registry Extract (where a public or government-accessible beneficial ownership register exists in the home jurisdiction)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille or government certification route, as applicable

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all directors, officers, shareholders and beneficial owners against the OFAC SDN List, UN Security Council Consolidated List, Canadian domestic sanctions under the Special Economic Measures Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act, and FINTRAC's guidance on politically exposed persons (PEPs). Enhanced due diligence is required for foreign PEPs, family members, and close associates. The screening must cover negative media, adverse regulatory actions, and sanctions exposure, with results documented in a compliance file retained for at least five years.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry (Service Alberta) – Online Company Registry
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: The proposed corporate name must be expressed in English or French characters (Roman alphabet) or using a recognized transliteration into the Roman alphabet. Names must be distinguishable from existing corporate and trade names on file with the Alberta Corporate Registry, must not be confusingly similar, and must not contain language likely to mislead. Legal elements such as 'Inc.', 'Corp.' or 'Ltd.' are mandatory where the name does not include 'Limited'. Non-Latin scripts must be transliterated as per established transliteration standards.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon name rejection, the applicant may file a written administrative appeal with the Director of Corporate Registry, Alberta Service Alberta, within 30 days of the rejection notice. The appeal must include the full reasons for rejection, an alternative name (where applicable), and evidence that the proposed name is distinguishable and non-confusing. If the administrative review is unsuccessful, the applicant may apply to the Court of King's Bench of Alberta for judicial review under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta). Before expiry, a name reservation may be extended for an additional 30-day period by filing an extension request and paying the applicable fee.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office address is permissible for administrative and business purposes for an e-commerce cosmetics retailer, but it cannot serve as the statutory registered office. The registered office must be a physical location in Alberta where corporate records are kept and legal notices may be served. A commercial registered agent may provide a service address for the statutory registered office; a virtual mailing address may be used separately for operational correspondence.

stage_1.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low for a standard e-commerce-only beauty retailer with no physical storefront. The estimated annual probability of an unannounced physical inspection of the registered office by the Alberta Corporate Registry is below 5%. The likelihood rises to approximately 20% if the company is selected for a CRA tax audit, FINTRAC AML compliance review, or upon a third-party complaint regarding corporate compliance. Inspections are generally triggered by red flags under applicable corporate, tax, or AML legislation rather than by routine screening.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9, as amended, ss. 5, 6, 7, 11, 23, 26, and 27 (as applicable).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Corporations, Alberta Corporate Registry (CORES), Service Alberta, Corporate Registry Operations.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation (Form 1) together with Notice of Registered Office (Form 2) and Notice of Directors (Form 3), filed through the Alberta Corporate Registration System (CORES).
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital requirement for Alberta business corporations. Shares may be issued at par value stated in the Articles of Incorporation; no escrow account or paid-up capital deposit is required under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta).
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: The undersigned, being the sole initial director of the Corporation, consents to and adopts the following resolutions effective upon issuance of the Certificate of Incorporation: (1) The subscription agreement for the Corporation's common shares is approved, and such shares are allotted and issued as set forth in the subscription records; (2) the registered office of the Corporation is established at [street address], in the City of [city], Province of Alberta, Canada; and (3) the following officers are appointed: [Name] as Chief Executive Officer, [Name] as Chief Financial Officer, and [Name] as Corporate Secretary. The officers are authorized to open bank accounts and complete all formalities.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Corporate Registry System (CORES) via authorized NUANS service providers.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a NUANS name search request through a registered CORES provider or the Alberta Corporate Registry portal. The search checks for conflicting trade names and distinguishes the proposed corporate name. Upon receiving a qualified NUANS report, pay the name reservation fee and obtain a Name Reservation Certificate valid for 90 calendar days, which will be used for the incorporation filing.
required_dossiers: Proposed corporate name (with legal element Inc., Corp., Ltd., etc.)
Consent of any third party whose name is relied upon
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is rejected for a conflict or non-distinctiveness, submit a new name reservation request using an alternative name from the NUANS report within the 90-day window, or request an administrative review by the Registrar within 14 days accompanied by evidence of acquired distinctiveness.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation and Notarization of Incorporation Documents
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Legal counsel, notary public, or authorized corporate service provider.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Draft the Articles of Incorporation in the exact Alberta Form 1 template, specifying share classes, director count, and restrictions. Prepare Form 2 (Notice of Registered Office) and Form 3 (Notice of Directors) together with consents by the named directors. Have the incorporator execute the documents before a notary public or in the presence of a witness as required. Where applicable, the signatures must be notarized to evidence authenticity for CORES submission.
required_dossiers: Consent to Act as Director (Form per Registry practice)
Notary or witness attestation of incorporator's signature
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registry identifies a substantive or typographical deficiency, the applicant will receive a Notice of Deficiency; the filer may amend and resubmit the corrected forms within 30 days without incurring a new filing fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Submission and Issuance of Certificate of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Corporations, Alberta Corporate Registry (CORES), Service Alberta.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: File the notarized incorporation package electronically through CORES or through an Alberta registry agent. Pay the statutory incorporation filing fee of CAD $400 (approximately USD $310) using the approved payment rails. The Registry reviews the articles for statutory compliance and, upon acceptance, issues the Certificate of Incorporation with the assigned corporate number and confirms the legal existence of the corporation.
required_dossiers: Payment receipt of statutory filing fee
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar refuses to issue the certificate, the applicant may request a written statement of reasons and file a revised application within 30 business days. If the refusal persists, the applicant may seek judicial review at the Court of King's Bench of Alberta.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First Board Resolution and Share Subscription
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the Corporation.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Following issuance of the Certificate of Incorporation, the initial director(s) execute the pro forma first board resolution, approving share subscriptions, adopting the registered office address, appointing officers, setting the fiscal year end, and authorizing corporate banking procedures. The share register and corporate minute book are opened at the registered office.
required_dossiers: Share subscription agreements and share certificate stubs
Consent of registered office landlord or service agreement
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If any officer appointment is later found invalid, the board may convene a special meeting and pass an omnibus corrective resolution ratifying the initial appointments, followed by an amended Notice of Directors filing.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Post-Incorporation Registrations and Corporate Book Completion
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA), Workers' Compensation Board (WCB) Alberta, and relevant municipal licensing authority.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Within three weeks of incorporation, register with the CRA for a Business Number (BN) using Form RC1, apply for the corporate income tax account, and register for GST/HST where annual revenue exceeds the CRA threshold. If the corporation will have employees, register for payroll deductions and WCB coverage. Obtain the applicable municipal business licence for online retail operations and complete the corporate statutory record filing.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA or provincial registrations are rejected due to missing information, the applicant will be notified and may correct and resubmit the specific account application within the statutory appeal windows. Late filings may be subject to administrative penalties under the Excise Tax Act and the Alberta Corporate Tax Act.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable — no industrial operating permit is required for an online retail business classified under ISIC 4791 / NAICS 456120 in Alberta.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No provincial or federal operating licence is mandated for the online retail sale of cosmetics. A municipal business licence may be required if there is a physical office or storage premises in a city such as Calgary or Edmonton under the Municipal Government Act, RSA 2000, c M-26.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Not applicable — Alberta Environmental Protection Agency (Alberta Environment and Protected Areas) does not engage for an online retail operation with no on-site industrial activity.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — no full or registered Environmental Impact Assessment is triggered.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: None applicable to the retail activity; general municipal waste management, recycling, and hazardous goods storage bylaws, if cosmetics include aerosol products, will be observed under the National Fire Code – Alberta Edition.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: No fire safety certification or structural load inspection is required for a pure online retail operation. If a commercial premises is occupied, the tenant must obtain landlord-provided fire safety compliance and, where employees are present, comply with the Occupational Health and Safety Act (Alberta), including a workplace hazard assessment, first-aid, and WCB registration.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC); online portal: CRA My Business Account and Canada Business Registration Online (BRO) platform.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Incorporating entity: register the 9-digit federal Business Number (BN) with CRA via BRO immediately after incorporation under the Canada Business Corporations Act or the Alberta Business Corporations Act; activate GST/HST 'RT' program account, corporate income tax 'RC' account and payroll 'RP' account in the same filing. Foreign entity without Canadian incorporation: submit non-resident BN and GST/HST registration through BRO, declaring Canadian carrying-on-business nexus (physical presence, agent, warehouse, or e-commerce supply of digital services); CRA issues the BN on the spot for most online applications and assigns a tax account that serves as the unified TIN for GST/HST, corporate income tax, payroll and customs purposes. Registration is mandatory once taxable supplies exceed CAD 30,000 in a calendar quarter or in the four preceding consecutive quarters; voluntary registration is available from the first transaction after nexus is established.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation — a Canadian corporation is a resident taxpayer separately assessed under Part I of the Income Tax Act on worldwide income; Alberta levies no provincial corporate income tax, so the effective federal rate is 15% general (9% on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income under the small business deduction); inter-corporate dividends are deductible to the recipient; no special attribution regime applies to active retail income; controlled foreign affiliate rules may apply where a foreign subsidiary earns passive income.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not operate a US check-the-box regime; entity classification follows the legal form of the organization. Statutory elections available to corporate taxpayers: (a) subsection 216(1) ITA election to report Canadian-source net rental income; (b) subsection 217 ITA election for non-residents to compute tax on Canadian employment income on the Part I basis; (c) joint GST/HST election under subsection 273(1) ETA to treat closely related corporations as a single registrant; (d) hybrid mismatch arrangement rules under Part I of the Income Tax Act (Budget Implementation Act 2022, effective for payments on or after July 1, 2023) which disallow deductions or impose inclusions to neutralize deduction/non-inclusion and double-deduction mismatches; no formal entity classification election is available to override the default corporate characterization.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST — federal Goods and Services Tax (GST) at 5%; Harmonized Sales Tax (HST) is not applicable in Alberta due to the absence of a provincial sales tax regime.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 — a supplier becomes a mandatory GST/HST registrant when worldwide taxable supplies by the entity and its associates exceed CAD 30,000 in one calendar quarter or in the four preceding consecutive quarters; small-supplier voluntary registration is available with an input tax credit recovery window starting one month before registration. Non-resident vendors supplying digital goods or services to Canadian residents must register and collect GST/HST without the small-supplier threshold under the July 1, 2021 simplified regime.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No statutory real-time clearance or digital stamping mandate. Canada operates a voluntary Pan-Canadian e-invoicing framework based on the Peppol BIS 3.0 standard; GST/HST returns must be filed electronically (GST/HST NETFILE) by registrants whose annual taxable supplies, including those of associates, exceed CAD 1,500,000. Audit-grade electronic document retention is mandatory; invoices are not pre-cleared by CRA but must be issued and retained in a legible, machine-readable format for the duration of the reassessment window.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Exports of tangible personal property, including cosmetics shipped to foreign consumers, are zero-rated under Schedule VI of the Excise Tax Act for supplies of goods delivered by the supplier or its agent to a destination outside Canada; retail direct-to-consumer export sales qualify if the supplier retains proof of export and the goods leave Canada within a reasonable time. Services performed wholly outside Canada and supplied to a non-resident who is not registered for GST/HST are also zero-rated; online orders fulfilled from a Canadian warehouse must have shipment documentation naming the foreign destination; no zero-rating is available for goods consumed in Canada.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration — CBSA B13A export report or electronic Canadian Export Declaration filed at the port of exit for commercial shipments
Bill of Lading, Waybill or courier proof of delivery (Canada Post, UPS, FedEx, DHL) showing export routing and foreign consignee address
Commercial invoice and purchase order or contract documenting the cosmetics product description, quantity, unit value, exporter identity and foreign customer
Inward Remittance Certificate or bank transfer / foreign exchange credit advice evidencing receipt of export proceeds in the corporate bank account within the repatriation window
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA may reassess GST/HST within four years of the date of the notice of assessment, and indefinitely for misrepresentation, fraud or wilful default, to claw back tax not substantiated; zero-rating documentation must be produced within 30 days of an export-verification audit request. False or grossly negligent claims trigger a penalty equal to the greater of CAD 250 and 25% of the tax understated under section 285 of the Excise Tax Act, plus prescribed daily-compounded arrears and instalment interest at CRA prescribed rates (currently 7% per annum). Knowingly false export zero-rating constitutes tax evasion under the Excise Tax Act and Income Tax Act, prosecutable as a criminal offence with fines up to 200% of tax evaded and imprisonment; CRA also applies export clawback red-flags where foreign receipts remain unrepatriated beyond 180 days.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), operating jointly with Payments Canada (clearing and settlement systems including LVTS, ACSS, and Real-Time Rail), the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) for bank prudential regulation, and FINTRAC for anti-money-laundering transaction reporting. Canada does not require any central-bank license or prior FX authorization for corporate treasury operations.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada operates under a fully convertible and free-floating exchange-rate regime for the Canadian dollar (CAD) pursuant to the Currency Act, following the repeal of the Foreign Exchange Control Act in 1951. There is no legal bifurcation between capital-account and current-account convertibility; profit remittance, dividend distributions, royalty payments, branch repatriations, and intercompany payments are unrestricted and do not require central-bank consent. Operational frictions are limited to (i) FINTRAC reporting obligations for all cross-border wire transfers of CAD 10,000 or more, (ii) Part XIII Income Tax Act withholding tax on non-resident remittances (statutory 25%, typically reduced under an applicable tax treaty), (iii) bank source-of-funds documentation for large inbound credits, and (iv) commercial FX spread and processing fees imposed by the clearing bank.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There is no statutory export-proceeds surrender requirement, no mandatory conversion timeline, and no fixed conversion ratio in Canada. An exporter of cosmetics and personal-care products may freely hold, convert, invest, or repatriate foreign-currency proceeds. Compliance obligations are confined to: (i) income-tax conversion of foreign receipts at the Bank of Canada daily published noon exchange rate, (ii) GST/HST zero-rating for qualifying exports under the Excise Tax Act, (iii) FINTRAC record-keeping and reporting thresholds (CAD 10,000) applicable to foreign currency exchange and cross-border electronic fund transfers, and (iv) customs audit obligations under the Customs Act (B3 export declarations for controlled or high-value outbound shipments).

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Royal Bank of Canada (RBC Royal Bank)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account (CAD settlement) plus USD foreign-currency account and FX hedging line
Capital Escrow Account and Operational Account integrated with TD Treasury and trade services
Operational Account with BMO Global Trade Finance and FX forward desk
Operational Account and UK/US corridor account for DTC cross-border retail settlement
Capital Escrow Account for non-resident equity injection and treasury concentration
Operational Account serving Alberta corporate clients with provincial footprint

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Low-to-Medium as a principal settlement bank. Offshore digital EMIs and neobanks cannot directly clear CAD obligations through Payments Canada LVTS unless they obtain Payments Canada membership or, in practice, rely on a Schedule I Canadian chartered bank sponsor. Under the Retail Payment Activities Act, payment service providers operating electronic-commerce payment functions in Canada must be registered or authorized with the Bank of Canada; unregistered operation is a statutory offence. Viability is acceptable for ancillary collection rails (Shopify Payments, PayPal, Wise Business) serving B2C card acceptance and USD payout, but the Alberta Corporation must maintain a Tier 1 federal bank account for CAD liquidity concentration, statutory escrow reconciliation, vendor disbursement, and confirmed FX execution.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical appearance is not statutorily mandated under the PCMLTFA and FINTRAC guidance; remote opening is available and widely accepted by Canadian Tier 1 banks. For an Alberta Business Corporation, the bank generally requires (i) a live video-based KYC interview with at least one director or senior officer, (ii) certified true copies of Articles of Incorporation, Certificate of Existence, Alberta registry search, share register, and register of directors, (iii) remote identity verification of all signatories using liveness detection and source-document verification, and (iv) a Canadian service address for corporate records. Non-resident beneficial owners with significant control are subject to enhanced due diligence, frequently requiring notarized or apostilled identity documents and tax-residence evidence; a physical branch visit is waived when the corporate ownership chain is fully transparent.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Shareholder composition involving offshore personal holding entities with an opaque beneficial-ownership chain
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: share register covering all issuances and transfers for the prior 24 months; annotated corporate organizational chart; certificates of incumbency and registered-agent certificates for each holding entity; register of directors and officers; beneficial-ownership schedule identifying every individual with a 25% or greater economic interest; certified passport copies and residential address evidence for all ultimate beneficial owners; FINTRAC-compliant beneficial-ownership declaration.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident directors or investors based in low-to-medium transparency jurisdictions
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: apostilled or legally certified passport copies; governmental utility or bank statements confirming residential address; tax-residence certificate or tax identification number; sworn declaration of source of initial capital and source of wealth; PEP and sanctions screening clearance; professional banker's reference or accountant's letter from the originating financial institution.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: E-commerce B2C transaction flow with elevated chargeback ratios or Shopify Payments / PayPal reconciliation variances
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: six months of payment-processor settlement statements showing gross sales, fees, refunds, and payout volumes; chargeback reason-code log and refund policy documentation; logistics contracts with courier providers (Canada Post, FedEx, DHL); commercial invoices and packing slips for export parcels; domain registration and website ownership proof; CRA business number and GST/HST registration confirmation; customer dispute resolution records.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Perceived mismatch between retail cosmetics activity and large cross-border supplier wires to manufacturing jurisdictions
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: executed supplier contracts and purchase orders; landed-cost and inventory reconciliation schedules; customs entry records from the Canada Border Services Agency; letters of credit or documentary collection documents evidencing the underlying purchase; monthly trial balance demonstrating wire values aligning with accounts payable; bank reference from the supplier's correspondent bank.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity injection from a non-resident shareholder is routed by SWIFT MT103 from the remitting bank to the Tier 1 Canadian bank account. The remittance narrative must specify 'inbound capital subscription - issuance of shares under the Canada Business Corporations Act' or 'paid-up capital contribution'. No Bank of Canada approval is required; the receiving bank performs OFAC sanctions screening, beneficial-ownership verification, and FINTRAC cross-border wire reporting where the amount equals or exceeds CAD 10,000. The source-of-funds dossier must include the board resolution authorizing the share issuance, the subscription agreement, the share certificate, the wire advice, and the paid-up-capital table. Profit repatriation by subsequent dividend is unrestricted but ordinarily subject to Part XIII withholding tax at 25% (treaty-reduced where applicable). For a shareholder-loan structure, a signed loan agreement and interest-rate schedule must be filed, with Part XIII interest-exemption criteria assessed for arm's-length and treaty-based lenders.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Trade disbursements for supplier settlement flow through standard Canadian clearing rails: (i) clean payments executed by SWIFT MT103 with fields 33B (settlement amount and currency), 50K (ordering customer), 59 (beneficiary bank and account), and 70 (remittance information referencing purchase order and commercial invoice); (ii) documentary commercial letters of credit issued under UCP600 via SWIFT MT700/MT701, with MT707 amendments and MT720 transfer for back-to-back arrangements; (iii) CAD interbank settlement through Payments Canada LVTS using Bank of Canada central-bank funds, with Real-Time Rail available for low-value immediate payments; and (iv) USD legs cleared through CHIPS or Fedwire via the Canadian bank's US correspondent. SWIFT GPI messaging provides end-to-end payment tracking. Inventory imports for cosmetics typically use 30- to 90-day open account terms or documentary collections aligned with the commercial invoice, packing list, and transport documents.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX forwards (CAD vs. USD, EUR, CNY) executed under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with a Tier 1 Canadian bank
Foreign exchange swaps (FX swap contracts) for short-dated liquidity deployment and rolling of settlement balances
Cross-currency interest rate swaps (CCIRS) exchanging principal and periodic interest flows on matched non-CAD liabilities
European-style plain-vanilla FX options (puts and calls) purchased for supplier-cost and revenue-side hedging
CME-listed CAD/USD currency futures as exchange-traded, centrally cleared hedging instruments
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) are legally permissible in Canada but operationally unnecessary for CAD given its free-floating fully convertible regime

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 14 days after the anniversary date of incorporation or the previous annual return filing date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Administrative strike-off from the corporate register after 90 days of delinquency; potential fines up to $500 plus daily penalties

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Mandatory independent audit required if the corporation is a distributing corporation or if total assets exceed $1,000,000 or gross revenue exceeds $500,000 in the preceding financial year

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: No annual beneficial ownership confirmation required; shareholding transfers do not trigger annual filings

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% combined general rate (15% federal Part I + 8% Alberta); 11% combined rate on the first CAD 500,000 of qualified active business income for a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) claiming the Small Business Deduction (9% federal + 2% Alberta).
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Small Business Deduction on active business income up to CAD 500,000 (business limit prorated across associated corporations); federal SR&ED refundable investment tax credit of 35% on qualified expenditures for CCPCs (15% non-refundable for large corporations); immediate expensing of specified depreciable capital assets; Alberta Film and Gaming tax credits and Capital Investment Incentive; foreign tax credit under s. 126 for foreign income taxes; treaty exemption/reduction of foreign-source business income.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return filed through CRA Corporation Internet Filing (T2 EFILE/Telex) via certified software (Ativa, Cantax, Profile, UFile) or mailed to CRA Calgary Tax Centre; all schedules (Schedules 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 400 and Alberta Schedules) integrated in the T2 package.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual (12-month fiscal period; a 53-week period is permitted for certain retail operations). Corporate income tax instalments are due quarterly on the 15th of the last month of each quarter; large corporations (taxable capital above CAD 15 million) use monthly instalments; balance of tax due is payable on the balance-due day, not on the T2 filing deadline.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: T2 return must be filed within 6 months after the fiscal year-end (calendar-year corporations: June 30 of the following year). Balance-due date: 2 months after fiscal year-end generally; 3 months for CCPCs eligible for the Small Business Deduction. Quarterly instalment dates: the last day of every complete quarter (months 3, 6, 9, 12 of the fiscal period).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Enter the 9-digit CRA business number (BN) plus the 'RP' program account and the fiscal year-end (YYYYMMDD).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation carrying on business in Canada must use its Canadian branch BN and identify the treaty jurisdiction of residence; complete the 'Non-resident' identification box.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tick the Alberta box to allocate taxable income to Alberta and compute provincial tax on Schedule 400.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations are taxable in Alberta only if they maintain a permanent establishment in Canada located in Alberta; determine allocation under the PE rules of the Canada-Alberta agreement.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Page 3 – Line 10 (Gross sales and other revenue)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Aggregate gross online retail sales, shipping fees and other revenue from cosmetics sales, before deductions; match to the audited income statement.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include only revenue attributable to the Canadian permanent establishment and Canadian-source e-commerce sales; exclude foreign-source revenue captured by the PE allocation formula.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Opening inventory plus purchases (including logistics and import duties) less closing inventory; detailed in Schedule 3.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: COGS attributable to the Canadian PE must be supported by customs/import documentation; related-party inventory purchases require arm's-length pricing and a TP Local File if thresholds are met.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Payroll expense, including T4 remuneration, bonuses, and employer NIC-style Canada Pension Plan/Employment Insurance contributions.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Reimburse head-office intercompany payroll charges strictly at cost; Canadian PE payroll must be allocated on actual time-and-effort data, not a markup.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: CCA computed on Schedule 8 using prescribed capital cost allowance classes (e.g., Class 10.1, Class 13, Class 50 for software); include half-year rule where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: CCA may be claimed only on depreciable property used in earning Canadian-source business income; head-office leased equipment requires apportionment.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Page 3 – Line 21 (Taxes other than income taxes)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Property taxes, Alberta health care contribution levy (AHCLP) and other deductible levies; income taxes themselves are non-deductible.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include only Alberta/Canadian municipal taxes attributable to the PE; foreign property taxes follow the treaty allocation formula.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Digital advertising, influencer compensation, Shopify platform fees and consumer acquisition costs.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Cross-border digital advertising fees paid to non-residents may be subject to Part XIII WHT at 25% (0% under the Canada-US treaty for certain advertising services not constituting a PE) and must be documented in Form T106.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Credit-card processing fees (Shopify Payments/PayPal), cloud-subscription fees, professional fees, bad debts and other ordinary retail expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Management fees paid to foreign parent companies are non-deductible without an arm's-length economic analysis and may attract Part XIII WHT of 25%; record NR301 forms from each non-resident payee.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net business income after all deductions; transferred to Schedule 1 to compute net income for tax purposes.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a non-resident, business income attributable to the Canadian PE is subject to Part I; foreign business income is excluded unless treaty-residence tie-breaker rules apply.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 1 – Lines 100/400 (Net income before and after adjustments)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Additions (e.g., 50% of non-eligible meals/entertainment, taxable dividends received, political contributions) and deductions (e.g., dividend deduction, non-capital loss carryovers) reconcile accounting net income to tax net income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Deductible amounts are limited to those reasonably regarded as wholly applicable to Canadian-source income; treaty-based deductions require explicit disclosure with Form T1134/T106 as applicable.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Alberta tax at 8% general rate (2% on the first CAD 500,000 active business income eligible for the SBD), applied to Alberta taxable income computed on the T2 provincial schedule.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Alberta tax applies only to the Alberta PE share of the corporation's taxable income under the provincial allocation formula; short-form provincial returns may be applicable for interprovincial allocations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal Part I tax at 38%, less the Provincial/Territorial abatement of 10%, the general corporate rate reduction and the SBD, yielding the 15% (or 9%) net federal rate.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The 10% provincial abatement is available only where a Canadian PE exists; non-residents without a PE in Canada cannot claim the abatement and may be subject to full Part I rate minus treaty protections.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing: 5% of unpaid balance plus 1% per full month (maximum 12 months), reaching 17%; repeated failure to file: 10% plus 2% per month. Late/insufficient instalments carry quarterly prescribed-rate interest (CRA corporate rate ~5-6%). Gross negligence for false statements: 50% of the understated tax; undisclosed reportable transactions: 50% with up to 25% non-disclosure penalty. Director liability attaches to unremitted payroll source deductions, GST/HST and Part XIII withholding, with CRA collection powers including garnishment, asset seizure, passport surrender orders for individuals, and restraining orders blocking departure.
